To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Vestibular-sensitive cerebellar granular layer neurons faithfully represent the direction and velocity of whole-body motion via bidirectional modulation, via bidirectional changes in the frequency of EPSCs.
synaptic inputs from the vestibular system to cerebellar granular cells encode stimulus velocity with high fidelity, and that this representation can be achieved with a small number of synapses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying sensory representation in the brain.
the neural basis of perception and action.
understanding the mechanisms underlying the processing of sensory information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a single neuron can encode the direction and velocity of whole-body motion via the frequency of excitatory synaptic input.

the vestibular system is able to detect and represent whole body movement, and that it does this with great precision and fidelity, and that it is able to do this with a relatively small number of sensory cells and a very small number of synapses.
the vestibular system has a high degree of sensitivity and precision.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vestibular system can be used to study the contribution of individual synaptic inputs to sensory representation in the cerebellum.
synaptic activity can signal sensory stimuli with a high degree of accuracy and resolution.
the vestibular system is a good model system for studying the neural representation of sensory information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
synaptic transmission is not a bottleneck for sensory representation.
synaptic transmission is not a limiting factor in the representation of a sensory stimulus by the nervous system.
sensory signals are faithfully transmitted by single synapses in vivo and the information is encoded in the number of synaptic inputs that are activated.
